title: Why Indian soymeal is losing buyers to Brazil and Argentina
subtitle: Oilmeal shipments from India fell by more than a quarter in April to August 2026, and soymeal shipments crashed by 73% on price.
content_html:
Picture two chai stalls side by side. One sells a cup for Rs 10, the other for Rs 14. Most people walk to the cheaper one. That simple rule just hit a big Indian export. On Monday, 9 November 2026, the solvent extractors' trade body (SEA) released data showing that oilmeal shipments from India fell to 12.82 lakh tonnes from April to August 2026, down from 17.93 lakh tonnes in the same months of 2025. That is more than a quarter gone in one year.

Soybean meal took the biggest hit. Shipments of it crashed by 73%. The reason is the chai stall rule: Indian soymeal cost a lot more than the soymeal sold by Brazil and Argentina, and buyers went where it was cheaper.

First, what is oilmeal?

Think of squeezing a lemon. You get juice, and the peel and pulp stay behind. Seeds like soybean, mustard and groundnut work the same way. Mills squeeze the oil out for cooking. What stays behind is a dry, crumbly powder full of protein. That is oilmeal.

Most soybean meal is made as a side product of taking oil out of soybeans, and it is mainly used in animal feed as a source of protein. It is a common feed for pigs and for chickens raised for meat and eggs. For scale, about 27.2 kg of soybeans gives about 21.8 kg of meal, so roughly four fifths of the bean ends up as meal.

How big was the fall?

Here are the main numbers the SEA shared for April to August 2026, as reported by the farm trade news site UkrAgroConsult:

  • All oilmeal: 12.82 lakh tonnes, against 17.93 lakh tonnes a year earlier. That is 5.11 lakh tonnes less.
  • Soybean meal: 2.05 lakh tonnes, against 7.57 lakh tonnes. A drop of 73%.
  • Rapeseed meal (made from mustard family seeds): 8.80 lakh tonnes, against 9.15 lakh tonnes. Only a small dip.

For the full 2025 to 2026 financial year, India shipped 37.68 lakh tonnes of oilmeal. So the first five months of this year are running well behind that pace.

Why did buyers walk away?

Price, mostly. The SEA said Indian soybean meal was trading at around $622 a tonne in August 2026, while the world benchmark price was near $445 a tonne. UkrAgroConsult worked out that this made the Indian product about $177 a tonne, or nearly 40%, more expensive. Importers turned to cheaper supplies from Brazil and Argentina.

This gap did not appear overnight. Back in May, Reuters reported (in a story carried by Datamar News) that Indian soymeal was being offered at around $680 a tonne, against $430 from South American sellers. Prices inside India had jumped 47% in a single month. Indian soybean output had fallen sharply because of bad weather, while poultry farms at home still wanted lots of meal.

One exporter, Vinod Jain, the founder of Suraj Impex, told Reuters plainly: "Buyers have switched to those countries."

The SEA also named two more problems:

  • Strong demand at home. Indian cattle and poultry feed makers bought a lot of meal, so less was left over to sell abroad.
  • Costly shipping. Trouble on Red Sea shipping routes and high sea freight charges made every tonne dearer to deliver.

Who still buys from India?

Not every buyer left. China, Bangladesh, South Korea and Vietnam were the biggest buyers of Indian oilmeal from April to August.

  • China: 4.01 lakh tonnes, up from 3.75 lakh tonnes. Almost all of it was rapeseed meal.
  • Bangladesh: about 2.17 lakh tonnes, up from about 1.78 lakh tonnes.
  • Vietnam: about 1.24 lakh tonnes, up from about 0.92 lakh tonnes.
  • South Korea: about 1.54 lakh tonnes, down from about 2.10 lakh tonnes.

Rapeseed meal made up nearly 69% of all Indian oilmeal shipments in these five months. It is now doing the heavy lifting, like a tail-end batter who keeps the score moving after the top order falls.

Indian soymeal has one special point. India grows soybeans that are not genetically modified (not changed in a lab), and Reuters noted that this usually earns Indian meal a higher price in places like Germany and the Netherlands. Even so, the export numbers show buyers switched this year.

What does this mean for farmers and feed makers?

For soybean farmers, high prices at home have a bright side. According to India Sea Trade News, the soybean processors' body SOPA said soybean prices in India stayed above the minimum support price (the floor price the government promises farmers) for most of the season. That helps farmers earn more for each sack.

The same high price is what makes the meal too costly abroad. The report noted that weaker soymeal exports could slow crushing work at Indian processing plants, even as demand from the poultry and animal feed industry at home stays firm.

For feed makers in India, the story cuts both ways. Their strong buying is one reason less meal was left to send abroad, the SEA said. But in May, Reuters reported that meal prices inside India had climbed 47% in a month, so feed makers were paying far more for the same sack.

This short video shows how a soy processing line separates soybean oil from the meal, the same split that sits at the heart of this story.

What happens next?

UkrAgroConsult said the outlook for Indian sellers depends on three things: the price fight with Brazil and Argentina, demand for feed inside India, and the cost of shipping by sea. If Indian soymeal stays far above the world price, shipments could stay low.

For a young trader or a student watching exports, the lesson from these numbers is short. In August 2026 Indian soymeal cost $177 a tonne more than the world benchmark, and even its non-GM premium did not keep buyers from switching. In bulk feed, the price per tonne did the talking.
